claim: HIV-1 assembles at the plasma membrane (PM) of infected cells.
source: HIV-1 assembles at the plasma membrane (PM) of infected cells.
evidence: This is a well-established fact stated in the abstract and introduction, supported by scientific consensus.

claim: PM association of the main structural protein Gag depends on its myristoylated MA domain and PM PI(4,5)P2.
source: PM association of the main structural protein Gag depends on its myristoylated MA domain and PM PI(4,5)P2.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and is a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Depletion of PI(4,5)P2 completely prevents Gag PM targeting and assembly site formation.
source: Using a novel chemical biology tool that allows rapidly tunable manipulation of PI(4,5)P2 levels in living cells, we show that depletion of PI(4,5)P2 completely prevents Gag PM targeting and assembly site formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1 and related text showing reduced Gag clusters upon PI(4,5)P2 depletion.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 depletion caused loss of pre-assembled Gag lattices from the PM.
source: Unexpectedly, PI(4,5)P2 depletion also caused loss of pre-assembled Gag lattices from the PM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 and Videos 6-7, demonstrating loss of Gag clusters upon rCD1 treatment.

claim: Restoration of PM PI(4,5)P2 reinduced assembly site formation even in the absence of new protein synthesis.
source: Subsequent restoration of PM PI(4,5)P2 reinduced assembly site formation even in the absence of new protein synthesis, indicating that the dissociated Gag molecules remained assembly competent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7 showing assembly site formation after FK506 treatment in the presence of cycloheximide.

claim: The dissociated Gag molecules remained assembly competent.
source: Subsequent restoration of PM PI(4,5)P2 reinduced assembly site formation even in the absence of new protein synthesis, indicating that the dissociated Gag molecules remained assembly competent.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that assembly sites reform after PI(4,5)P2 restoration without new protein synthesis.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 has an important role for HIV-1 morphogenesis beyond Gag recruitment to the PM.
source: These results reveal an important role of PI(4,5)P2 for HIV-1 morphogenesis beyond Gag recruitment to the PM and suggest a dynamic equilibrium of Gag-lipid interactions.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that pre-assembled Gag lattices dissociate upon PI(4,5)P2 depletion.

claim: There is a dynamic equilibrium of Gag-lipid interactions.
source: These results reveal an important role of PI(4,5)P2 for HIV-1 morphogenesis beyond Gag recruitment to the PM and suggest a dynamic equilibrium of Gag-lipid interactions.
evidence: This is suggested based on the reversible nature of Gag membrane association observed in the experiments.

claim: The experimental system permits synchronized induction of HIV-1 assembly leading to induced production of infectious virions.
source: Furthermore, they establish an experimental system that permits synchronized induction of HIV-1 assembly leading to induced production of infectious virions by targeted modulation of Gag PM targeting.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2-5 showing synchronized assembly and production of infectious virus.

claim: HIV-1 particles assemble and bud at the plasma membrane (PM) of infected cells.
source: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) particles assemble and bud at the plasma membrane (PM) of infected cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: Gag trafficking from cytosolic polysomes to the inner leaflet of the PM is required for HIV-1 assembly.
source: This requires trafficking of the main structural component Gag from its site of synthesis at cytosolic polysomes to the inner leaflet of the PM.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV-1 assembly process.

claim: Gag assembles into a multimeric lattice comprising ~2500 Gag molecules at the PM.
source: Here, Gag assembles into a multimeric lattice comprising ~2500 Gag molecules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV-1 assembly cited in the introduction.

claim: Gag recruits other constituents of the infectious virion and ESCRT components to nascent budding sites.
source: Gag also recruits the other constituents of the infectious virion as well as components of the cellular endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT) to nascent budding sites (reviewed in Sundquist and Kräusslich, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Gag consists of the individually folded MA, CA, NC and p6 domains.
source: Gag consists of the individually folded MA (matrix), CA (capsid), NC (nucleocapsid) and p6 domains, which separate upon proteolytic maturation to the infectious virion.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about HIV-1 Gag protein.

claim: MA, CA, NC and p6 domains separate upon proteolytic maturation to the infectious virion.
source: Gag consists of the individually folded MA (matrix), CA (capsid), NC (nucleocapsid) and p6 domains, which separate upon proteolytic maturation to the infectious virion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV-1 maturation.

claim: CA and NC mediate protein and RNA interactions during virion morphogenesis.
source: CA and NC mediate protein and RNA interactions during virion morphogenesis, while p6 recruits ESCRT components.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the functions of Gag domains.

claim: p6 recruits ESCRT components.
source: CA and NC mediate protein and RNA interactions during virion morphogenesis, while p6 recruits ESCRT components.
evidence: This is established knowledge about p6 function.

claim: PM targeting of Gag depends on the N-terminal MA domain.
source: PM targeting of Gag depends on the N-terminal MA domain.
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The N-terminal myristoyl moiety and a surface exposed patch of basic residues in MA (the highly basic region, HBR) are important for Gag targeting, membrane association and virus formation.
source: Mutational analyses revealed that the N-terminal myristoyl moiety and a surface exposed patch of basic residues in MA (the highly basic region, HBR) are important for Gag targeting, membrane association and virus formation (Lorizate and Kräusslich, 2011; Freed, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mutational studies.

claim: The N-terminal myristoyl moiety and HBR alone would not be sufficient to explain specific PM targeting.
source: However, these two features would not be sufficient to explain specific PM targeting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the need for additional specificity factors like PI(4,5)P2.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 acts as a cue for specific recruitment of many peripheral PM proteins.
source: The phosphoinositide phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) is known to act as a cue for specific recruitment of many peripheral PM proteins and was also shown to be important for Gag PM targeting.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PI(4,5)P2 function.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is important for Gag PM targeting.
source: The phosphoinositide phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) is known to act as a cue for specific recruitment of many peripheral PM proteins and was also shown to be important for Gag PM targeting.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Depleting PI(4,5)P2 abolished PM targeting of Gag.
source: Depleting PI(4,5)P2 abolished PM targeting of Gag, while increasing PI(4,5)P2 at intracellular membranes redirected Gag to those sites (Ono et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ono et al., 2004.

claim: Increasing PI(4,5)P2 at intracellular membranes redirected Gag to those sites.
source: Depleting PI(4,5)P2 abolished PM targeting of Gag, while increasing PI(4,5)P2 at intracellular membranes redirected Gag to those sites (Ono et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ono et al., 2004.

claim: Presence of PI(4,5)P2 enhances binding of Gag-derived proteins to synthetic liposomes in vitro.
source: Consistently, several studies reported that presence of PI(4,5)P2 enhances binding of Gag-derived proteins to synthetic liposomes in vitro (Chukkapalli et al., 2008, 2010; Dick et al., 2012; Olety and Ono, 2014; Mercredi et al., 2016), and PI(4,5)P2 appeared to be enriched in the HIV-1 lipidome (Chan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to in vitro studies.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 appeared to be enriched in the HIV-1 lipidome.
source: Consistently, several studies reported that presence of PI(4,5)P2 enhances binding of Gag-derived proteins to synthetic liposomes in vitro (Chukkapalli et al., 2008, 2010; Dick et al., 2012; Olety and Ono, 2014; Mercredi et al., 2016), and PI(4,5)P2 appeared to be enriched in the HIV-1 lipidome (Chan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chan et al., 2008.

claim: Gag dominates in a monomeric form or in small oligomers in the cytoplasm.
source: Gag seems to dominate in a monomeric form or in small oligomers in the cytoplasm (Kutluay and Bieniasz, 2010; Hendrix et al., 2015), and its N-terminal myristate group is proposed to be buried within the globular domain of MA at this stage (Spearman et al., 1997; Saad et al., 2006; Tang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The N-terminal myristate group of Gag is proposed to be buried within the globular domain of MA in the cytoplasm.
source: Gag seems to dominate in a monomeric form or in small oligomers in the cytoplasm (Kutluay and Bieniasz, 2010; Hendrix et al., 2015), and its N-terminal myristate group is proposed to be buried within the globular domain of MA at this stage (Spearman et al., 1997; Saad et al., 2006; Tang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a proposed model supported by citations.

claim: Gag interaction with PI(4,5)P2 has been suggested to trigger exposure of the myristate moiety followed by its insertion into the inner leaflet of the PM.
source: Gag interaction with PI(4,5)P2 has been suggested to trigger exposure of the myristate moiety followed by its insertion into the inner leaflet of the PM, thereby anchoring Gag.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on previous studies.

claim: Recent models propose a regulatory role of RNA for the myristoyl switch.
source: Recent models propose a regulatory role of RNA for this myristoyl switch (Chukkapalli et al., 2010; Alfadhli et al., 2011; Chukkapalli et al., 2013; Kutluay et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent modeling studies.

claim: In the cytosol, specific cellular tRNAs are bound to the basic region of MA in the absence of PI(4,5)P2, preventing premature Gag association with intracellular membranes.
source: In the cytosol, specific cellular tRNAs are bound to the basic region of MA in the absence of PI(4,5)P2, thus preventing premature Gag association with intracellular membranes.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on cited studies.

claim: MA-tRNA interaction may be outcompeted by PI(4,5)P2 at the PM, triggering the myristoyl switch.
source: This MA-tRNA interaction may be outcompeted by PI(4,5)P2 at the PM, thereby triggering the myristoyl switch.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the tRNA competition model.

claim: The NMR structure of HIV-1 MA bound to PI(4,5)P2 revealed the 2´ acyl chain to be buried in the myristoyl-binding pocket of MA.
source: The NMR structure of HIV-1 MA bound to a PI(4,5)P2 molecule carrying truncated acyl chains revealed the 2´ acyl chain to be buried in the myristoyl-binding pocket of MA (Saad et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an NMR structure study.

claim: The NMR structure observation suggested a model for Gag membrane anchoring that was subsequently challenged.
source: This observation suggested a model for Gag membrane anchoring, which was subsequently challenged by a recent report from the same group, however (Mercredi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations showing evolution of the model.

claim: Upon arrival of Gag at the PM, the 2´ acyl chain of PI(4,5)P2 may be flipped outward and displace myristate from the acyl binding pocket of MA.
source: Upon arrival of Gag at the PM, the 2´ acyl chain of PI(4,5)P2 may be flipped outward and displace myristate from the acyl binding pocket of MA.
evidence: This is a proposed model from cited literature.

claim: Myristate would insert into the PM after being displaced from the MA pocket.
source: Myristate in turn would insert into the PM.
evidence: This is part of the proposed lipid flip model.

claim: Exchange of the unsaturated 2´ acyl chain of PI(4,5)P2 by saturated myristic acid would increase local lipid saturation and membrane order.
source: The consequent exchange of the unsaturated 2´ acyl chain of PI(4,5)P2 by the saturated myristic acid would increase local lipid saturation and membrane order.
evidence: This is a proposed consequence of the lipid flip mechanism.

claim: The lipid flip mechanism could explain the observed liquid-ordered state of the HIV envelope.
source: If occurring in all or a majority of the ~2500 tightly packed Gag molecules, this mechanism could also explain the observed liquid-ordered state of the HIV envelope (Lorizate et al., 2009; Brügger et al., 2006; Chan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation connecting the lipid flip model to observed envelope properties.

claim: The lipid flip model would suggest that Gag clusters are stably anchored to the PM via their myristoyl moiety.
source: This model would further suggest that Gag clusters are stably anchored to the PM via their myristoyl moiety and PI(4,5)P2 would then be expected to be dispensable once anchoring has occurred.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the lipid flip model.

claim: According to the lipid flip model, PI(4,5)P2 would be dispensable once Gag anchoring has occurred.
source: This model would further suggest that Gag clusters are stably anchored to the PM via their myristoyl moiety and PI(4,5)P2 would then be expected to be dispensable once anchoring has occurred.
evidence: This is a prediction from the lipid flip model that the current study tests.

claim: The dynamics of PI(4,5)P2 Gag interaction and the role of PI(4,5)P2 in later stages of HIV assembly have not been examined prior to this study.
source: PI(4,5)P2 is clearly important for Gag PM targeting, but the dynamics of PI(4,5)P2 Gag interaction and the role of PI(4,5)P2 in later stages of HIV assembly have not been examined so far.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The rCDS allows rapid and controlled depletion and reconstitution of PM PI(4,5)P2 levels in living cells.
source: Here, we made use of a recently developed reversible chemical dimerizer system (abbreviated rCDS) allowing rapid and controlled depletion and reconstitution of PM PI(4,5)P2 levels in living, virus-producing cells by a small molecule (Feng et al., 2014; Schifferer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the development of the rCDS system.

claim: The nascent HIV-1 Gag assembly site is highly dependent on PI(4,5)P2 during the entire assembly process.
source: Using this system, we showed that the nascent HIV-1 Gag assembly site is highly dependent on PI(4,5)P2 during the entire assembly process, and membrane association of apparently complete assembly sites remained PI(4,5)P2 dependent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing loss of assembly sites upon PI(4,5)P2 depletion.

claim: Membrane association of apparently complete assembly sites remained PI(4,5)P2 dependent.
source: Using this system, we showed that the nascent HIV-1 Gag assembly site is highly dependent on PI(4,5)P2 during the entire assembly process, and membrane association of apparently complete assembly sites remained PI(4,5)P2 dependent.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 showing loss of pre-formed assembly sites.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 removal from the PM caused dissociation of pre-assembled Gag clusters from the membrane.
source: PI(4,5)P2 removal from the PM not only abolished Gag PM targeting, but also caused dissociation of pre-assembled Gag clusters from the membrane.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Reconstitution of bona fide Gag assembly sites at the PM was observed upon re-establishment of PM PI(4,5)P2 levels.
source: Reconstitution of bona fide Gag assembly sites at the PM was observed upon re-establishment of PM PI(4,5)P2 levels.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 6-8 showing assembly site reformation.

claim: The findings are inconsistent with stable anchoring of large Gag clusters at the PM through myristoyl moieties alone.
source: Our findings are inconsistent with stable anchoring of large Gag clusters at the PM through myristoyl moieties alone and suggest a highly dynamic mode of Gag PM binding.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that pre-assembled clusters dissociate upon PI(4,5)P2 depletion.

claim: The findings suggest a highly dynamic mode of Gag PM binding.
source: Our findings are inconsistent with stable anchoring of large Gag clusters at the PM through myristoyl moieties alone and suggest a highly dynamic mode of Gag PM binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the reversible nature of Gag membrane association.

claim: The approach allows synchronization of assembly and release of infectious HIV-1.
source: Furthermore, this approach allows synchronization of assembly and release of infectious HIV-1.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2-5 showing synchronized assembly and infectious virus production.

claim: HIV-1 assembly and release processes are usually highly asynchronous, both within a cell population and on the level of individual cells.
source: These processes are usually highly asynchronous, both within a cell population and on the level of individual cells (Ivanchenko et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PM recruitment of the phosphatase was complete within 5 min after rCD1 addition.
source: Under our conditions, PM recruitment of the phosphatase was complete within 5 min after rCD1 addition.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system characterization.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 depletion can be monitored through dissociation from the PM of an EGFP-tagged pleckstrin homology (PH) domain of PLCδ.
source: PI(4,5)P2 depletion can be monitored through dissociation from the PM of an EGFP-tagged pleckstrin homology (PH) domain of PLCδ; its dissociation was observed as early as 2 min after rCD1 addition in HeLa cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Video 1.

claim: Dissociation of the PH-domain reporter was observed as early as 2 min after rCD1 addition in HeLa cells.
source: PI(4,5)P2 depletion can be monitored through dissociation from the PM of an EGFP-tagged pleckstrin homology (PH) domain of PLCδ; its dissociation was observed as early as 2 min after rCD1 addition in HeLa cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PM recruitment of the Enzyme can be reversed by adding the rCD1 competitor FK506.
source: PM recruitment of the Enzyme can be reversed by adding the rCD1 competitor FK506 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is part of the rCDS system design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: FK506 outcompetes the binding of rCD1 to the FKBP domain causing removal of the Enzyme from the PM within seconds.
source: FK506 outcompetes the binding of rCD1 to the FKBP domain causing removal of the Enzyme from the PM within seconds and replenishment of normal PI(4,5)P2 levels by endogenous PI(4)P5 kinases.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the rCDS reversal.

claim: Full re-localization of the PH-domain reporter to the PM was detected 2 min after addition of FK506.
source: Full re-localization of the PH-domain reporter to the PM was detected 2 min after addition of FK506, indicating rapid and efficient recovery of PI(4,5)P2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: rCD1 addition at 4 hr after transfection caused an 80% reduction of Gag clusters at the ventral PM compared to control cells.
source: Quantification of Gag clusters at the ventral PM of DMSO (n = 27) or rCD1 treated (n = 26) cells revealed a pronounced (80%) and highly significant (p<0.0001) reduction of Gag clusters in PM PI(4,5)P2 depleted cells compared to control cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is quantitative data from Figure 1F.

claim: The reduction of Gag clusters upon PI(4,5)P2 depletion was highly significant (p<0.0001).
source: Quantification of Gag clusters at the ventral PM of DMSO (n = 27) or rCD1 treated (n = 26) cells revealed a pronounced (80%) and highly significant (p<0.0001) reduction of Gag clusters in PM PI(4,5)P2 depleted cells compared to control cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of the data in Figure 1F.

claim: Interaction of Gag with PI(4,5)P2 in vitro is mediated by the N-terminal MA domain.
source: Interaction of Gag with PI(4,5)P2 in vitro is mediated by the N-terminal MA domain and mutations in MA affect Gag PM localization.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous in vitro studies.

claim: Mutations in MA affect Gag PM localization.
source: Interaction of Gag with PI(4,5)P2 in vitro is mediated by the N-terminal MA domain and mutations in MA affect Gag PM localization.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous mutational studies.

claim: Gag(Δ8–126 SR) retains the myristoylation signal and C-terminal cleavage site but carries a deletion of the entire globular MA domain.
source: In order to gain further insight into the role of MA for the observed PI(4,5)P2-dependent Gag recruitment, we employed a Gag variant that retains the myristoylation signal and C-terminal cleavage site, but carries a deletion of the entire globular MA domain (Δ8–126 SR).
evidence: This describes the design of the MA deletion construct used in the study.

claim: Gag(Δ8–126 SR) has been shown to assemble both at the PM and at intracellular membranes of MT-4 cells.
source: This protein has been shown to assemble both at the PM and at intracellular membranes of MT-4 cells and is competent for particle release (Reil et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reil et al., 1998.

claim: Gag(Δ8–126 SR) is competent for particle release.
source: This protein has been shown to assemble both at the PM and at intracellular membranes of MT-4 cells and is competent for particle release (Reil et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reil et al., 1998.

claim: PM localization and assembly site formation of Gag(Δ8–126 SR) was not affected by PI(4,5)P2 depletion.
source: As can be seen in Figure 1C, PM localization and assembly site formation of Gag(Δ8–126 SR) was not affected by PI(4,5)P2 depletion.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and quantified in Figure 1F.

claim: Quantification of Gag(Δ8–126 SR) clusters showed no statistically significant difference upon PI(4,5)P2 depletion (p=0.8392).
source: Quantification of Gag clusters in DMSO (n = 15) or rCD1 treated (n = 18) cells showed no statistically significant difference in the number of Gag clusters at the ventral PM upon PI(4,5)P2 depletion (p=0.8392) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of data in Figure 1F.

claim: The results provide direct evidence for the requirement of the globular MA domain for PI(4,5)P2 dependent Gag recruitment to the PM.
source: These results provide direct evidence for the requirement of the globular MA domain for PI(4,5)P2 dependent Gag recruitment to the PM.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the MA deletion experiments.

claim: Changing MA residues K25,K26 to T25,T26 was reported to exhibit enhanced PI(4,5)P2 independent membrane binding.
source: Changing MA residues K25,K26 to T25,T26 was reported to exhibit enhanced PI(4,5)P2 independent membrane binding (Chukkapalli et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chukkapalli et al., 2010.

claim: PM recruitment and assembly site formation of the 25/26KT variant was not significantly affected by PI(4,5)P2 depletion in live cells (p=0.1242).
source: Consistent with this in vitro observation, PM recruitment and assembly site formation of the 25/26KT variant was not significantly affected by PI(4,5)P2 depletion in live cells (p=0.1242) (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: Changing MA residues K29,K31 to E29,E31 had been reported to cause complete loss of PI(4,5)P2 sensitivity with Gag mislocalization and impaired virus release.
source: Changing MA residues K29,K31 to E29,E31 had been reported to cause complete loss of PI(4,5)P2 sensitivity with Gag mislocalization and impaired virus release; virus production was partially restored upon an additional change of MA residue E16 to K16 (Tedbury et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tedbury et al., 2015.

claim: Virus production of the 29/31KE variant was partially restored upon an additional change of MA residue E16 to K16.
source: Changing MA residues K29,K31 to E29,E31 had been reported to cause complete loss of PI(4,5)P2 sensitivity with Gag mislocalization and impaired virus release; virus production was partially restored upon an additional change of MA residue E16 to K16 (Tedbury et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tedbury et al., 2015.

claim: The 16EK mutation correlated with enhanced membrane binding of the MA variant in vitro, but did not appear to restore PI(4,5)P2 dependence.
source: This correlated with enhanced membrane binding of the MA variant in vitro, but the additional mutation did not appear to restore PI(4,5)P2 dependence (Tedbury et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tedbury et al., 2015.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 depletion did not have a statistically significant effect on assembly of 16EK 29/31KE Gag (p=0.5948).
source: In agreement with these results, we observed that PI(4,5)P2 depletion did not have a statistically significant effect on assembly of 16EK 29/31KE Gag (p=0.5948) (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: At 22 hr after transfection with PI(4,5)P2 depletion, Gag-EGFP was found to be mainly cytosolic with very few Gag assemblies at the PM.
source: At 22 hr after transfection, Gag-EGFP was found to be mainly cytosolic with very few Gag assemblies at the PM (Figure 2A, left panel).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 2A.

claim: Addition of FK506 and consequent restoration of PM PI(4,5)P2 levels rapidly induced Gag cluster formation at the PM.
source: Addition of FK506 and consequent restoration of PM PI(4,5)P2 levels rapidly induced Gag cluster formation at the PM (Figure 2A and C and Video 2), whereas no major changes were observed upon addition of DMSO (Figure 2B and C, Video 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A, C and Video 2.

claim: No major changes in Gag cluster formation were observed upon addition of DMSO control.
source: Addition of FK506 and consequent restoration of PM PI(4,5)P2 levels rapidly induced Gag cluster formation at the PM (Figure 2A and C and Video 2), whereas no major changes were observed upon addition of DMSO (Figure 2B and C, Video 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B, C and Video 3.

claim: After 90 min of FK506 treatment, the ventral PMs were covered with nascent HIV assembly sites and/or particles trapped between the cell and the coverslip.
source: After 90 min of FK506 treatment, the ventral PMs were covered with nascent HIV assembly sites and/or particles trapped between the cell and the coverslip (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 2A.

claim: Assembly site formation at the PM was not impaired for the MA deletion variant Δ8–126 SR in PM PI(4,5)P2 depleted cells.
source: Analogous experiments performed with the MA deletion variant Δ8–126 SR confirmed dependence of the PI(4,5)P2 responsive phenotype on the MA domain of Gag. Assembly site formation at the PM was not impaired for this variant in PM PI(4,5)P2 depleted cells, and no significant difference was observed between cells subsequently treated with FK506 or DMSO (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant difference in assembly was observed for Δ8–126 SR between cells treated with FK506 or DMSO.
source: Analogous experiments performed with the MA deletion variant Δ8–126 SR confirmed dependence of the PI(4,5)P2 responsive phenotype on the MA domain of Gag. Assembly site formation at the PM was not impaired for this variant in PM PI(4,5)P2 depleted cells, and no significant difference was observed between cells subsequently treated with FK506 or DMSO (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of the globular MA domain makes Gag independent of and unresponsive to PI(4,5)P2.
source: Deletion of the globular MA domain thus makes Gag independent of and unresponsive to PI(4,5)P2.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the MA deletion experiments.

claim: Mean assembly rate constants did not differ significantly between induced and native assembly, with k = 4.5 ± 0.47*10−3 s−1 for native and k = 3.49 ± 0.26*10−3 s−1 for induced assembly sites (p=0.8563).
source: Mean assembly rate constants derived from averaging all individual k values did not differ significantly between induced and native assembly, with k = 4.5 ± 0.47*10−3 s−1 for native and k = 3.49 ± 0.26*10−3 s−1 for induced assembly sites (p=0.8563) and a similar distribution of rate constants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is quantitative analysis from TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The assembly rate constants translate into half-times of approximately 150 s and 200 s for native and induced assembly, respectively.
source: This translates into half-times of approximately 150 s and 200 s for native and induced assembly, respectively, or 8.5 min and 11 min for 90% completion of native and induced assembly, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the assembly rate constants.

claim: The assembly half-time values are in agreement with previously published data.
source: This translates into half-times of approximately 150 s and 200 s for native and induced assembly, respectively, or 8.5 min and 11 min for 90% completion of native and induced assembly, respectively. These values are in agreement with previously published data (Ivanchenko et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ivanchenko et al., 2009.

claim: PM accumulation of assembly sites occurred more rapidly for induced compared to native assembly sites.
source: Visual inspection of the movies suggested that PM accumulation of assembly sites occurred more rapidly for induced compared to native assembly sites, while assembly rates at individual sites did not significantly differ between the two conditions.
evidence: This is an observation from visual inspection of microscopy movies.

claim: Formation of 100 new assembly sites per 1000 µm2 PM required only ~15 min for induced versus 45 min for native assembly.
source: Figure 3D shows that assembly sites accumulated faster and more synchronously when induced by PI(4,5)P2 restoration compared to the native situation. Formation of 100 new assembly sites per 1000 µm2 PM required only ~15 min for induced versus 45 min for native assembly.
evidence: This is quantitative data from Figure 3D.

claim: Assembly sites accumulated faster and more synchronously when induced by PI(4,5)P2 restoration compared to the native situation.
source: Figure 3D shows that assembly sites accumulated faster and more synchronously when induced by PI(4,5)P2 restoration compared to the native situation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: STED nanoscopy strongly increased resolution compared to confocal images and HIV-1 assembly subdomains became discernible.
source: As can be seen in Figure 4, STED nanoscopy strongly increased resolution compared to confocal images and HIV-1 assembly subdomains became discernible (compare confocal and STED panels).
evidence: This is shown by comparison of confocal and STED panels in Figure 4.

claim: Neither the overall appearance of the cell nor the spatial distribution of Gag and Env at late assemblies differed notably between native and induced assembly.
source: STED images revealed that neither the overall appearance of the cell nor the spatial distribution of Gag and Env at late assemblies differed notably between native and induced assembly.
evidence: This is an observation from STED imaging in Figure 4.

claim: Both native and induced structures were characterized by a densely-packed Gag cluster with a diameter of about 120 nm, surrounded by a clustered accumulation of Env.
source: Both structures were characterized by a densely-packed Gag cluster with a diameter of about 120 nm, surrounded by a clustered accumulation of Env (Figure 4), in line with previous observations (Muranyi et al., 2013; Roy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: The morphology of induced late assemblies was indistinguishable from native sites in micrographs as well as in averaged line profiles of individual assemblies.
source: The morphology of induced late assemblies was indistinguishable from native sites in micrographs (compare Figure 4A and B) as well as in averaged line profiles of individual assemblies (compare Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is shown by comparison of Figure 4A-D.

claim: HeLarCDS cells constitutively express both the Anchor and Enzyme fusion proteins.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, HeLarCDS cells constitutively express both fusion proteins, with the Enzyme detected in the cytoplasm and the Anchor at the PM.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The rCDS is functional in HeLarCDS cells as demonstrated by PI(4,5)P2 indicator localization.
source: Next, we assessed functionality of the rCDS in these cells by expressing EGFP-PLCδ-PH, whose PM localization serves as indicator for PI(4,5)P2. In the absence of rCD1, the indicator was detected mainly at the PM (Figure 5B, left panel). Upon rCD1 addition (Figure 5B, middle panel), the Enzyme translocated to the PM (see insert), resulting in relocalization of the indicator protein to the cytoplasm as a consequence of PI(4,5)P2 depletion from the PM. This effect was reversed upon addition of FK506 (Figure 5B, right panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 depletion caused an 80–85% reduction in virus production compared to control cells.
source: Comparing virus production from rCD1 and control cells at 22 hr after transfection showed a strong inhibition by PI(4,5)P2 depletion (80–85% reduction compared to control cells) (Figure 5C; see also Figure 5—figure supplement 1A for non-normalized data).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Virus production was restored after FK506 addition.
source: Virus assembly was then induced in rCD1-treated cells by addition of 1 µM FK506 at 22 hr after transfection. Extracellular virus was collected 2 hr after addition of FK506 since a short harvest time limits the analysis mainly to virions formed by induced assembly. Virus production was restored after FK506 addition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Relative infectivity of virions produced under inducing conditions was only mildly reduced (~65% compared to virions produced under native conditions).
source: Most importantly, relative infectivity of virions produced under inducing conditions was only mildly reduced (~65% compared to virions produced under native conditions from DMSO treated HeLarCDS cells) (Figure 5D; see also Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C for non-normalized data).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Induced PM recruitment of Gag allows faithful assembly of infectious HIV-1 particles.
source: These results indicate that induced PM recruitment of Gag allows faithful assembly of infectious HIV-1 particles.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the infectivity data in Figure 5.

claim: The vast majority of cells (52 of 59) lost most pre-formed Gag assemblies from the lateral PM upon PI(4,5)P2 depletion.
source: Unexpectedly, the vast majority of cells (52 of 59) lost most pre-formed Gag assemblies from the lateral PM upon PI(4,5)P2 depletion (Figure 6A and Video 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and Video 6.

claim: The number of Gag clusters decreased to 50% at ~30 min after rCD1 addition and reached a minimum level of ~30%.
source: For quantitative analysis, we determined the relative number of Gag clusters over time following PI(4,5)P2 depletion in the cell shown in Figure 6A (Figure 6C). This number decreased to 50% at ~30 min after rCD1 addition and reached a minimum level of ~30%.
evidence: This is quantitative data from Figure 6C.

claim: DMSO treated cells retained or slowly increased the number of Gag assembly sites at the lateral PM over time.
source: In contrast, DMSO treated cells retained or slowly increased the number of Gag assembly sites at the lateral PM over time (Figure 6C and E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Video 7), excluding any unspecific effect of the carrier or the imaging procedure.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C, E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, and Video 7.

claim: PM PI(4,5)P2 depletion had no effect on preformed assembly sites for the Δ8–126 SR Gag variant.
source: PM PI(4,5)P2 depletion also had no effect on preformed assembly sites for the Δ8–126 SR Gag variant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C), and this was confirmed by quantitative analysis of Gag(Δ8–126 SR) cluster number over time (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C, and D.

claim: FK506 treatment yielded a rapid increase in the number of Gag assembly sites at the PM after PI(4,5)P2 depletion.
source: For this experiment, we treated cells displaying pre-formed assembly sites with rCD1 for 90 min as described above, followed by addition of FK506 to allow PM PI(4,5)P2 reconstitution. FK506 treatment yielded a rapid increase in the number of Gag assembly sites at the PM (Figure 6B, Video 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and Video 6.

claim: The number of Gag clusters reached the initial level (prior to rCD1 mediated PI(4,5)P2 depletion) at 30–40 min after addition of FK506.
source: The number of Gag clusters reached the initial level (prior to rCD1 mediated PI(4,5)P2 depletion) at 30–40 min after addition of FK506 (Figure 6D and F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and F.

claim: No effect on the number of Gag clusters was observed in control cells treated with DMSO after PI(4,5)P2 depletion.
source: No effect on the number of Gag clusters was observed in control cells treated with DMSO (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Figure 6D and F, Video 7) or when the PI(4,5)P2 independent MA variant Δ8–126 SR was used (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C and E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Figure 6D and F, and Video 7.

claim: Newly induced assembly sites generally did not appear at those positions where previously dissociated sites had been observed.
source: Visual inspection of movie sequences indicated that newly induced assembly sites generally did not appear at those positions where previously dissociated sites had been observed.
evidence: This is an observation from visual inspection of microscopy movies.

claim: Accumulation of reinduced HIV-1 Gag assemblies following a cycle of PI(4,5)P2 depletion and restoration occurred twice as fast as initial accumulation of budding sites under induced conditions.
source: Quantitative analyses indicated that accumulation of reinduced HIV-1 Gag assemblies following a cycle of PI(4,5)P2 depletion and restoration (Figure 6D and F) occurred twice as fast as initial accumulation of budding sites under induced conditions (compare Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a comparison of quantitative data from Figures 6D, F and 2C.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 depletion resulted in loss of clusters from the PM that was fully reverted by restoring PI(4,5)P2 levels in the presence of CHX.
source: To analyze whether reinduced Gag assembly sites at the PM upon PI(4,5)P2 reconstitution comprised only newly synthesized Gag molecules or whether 'recycled' molecules previously depleted from the membrane contribute, we blocked protein translation by cycloheximide (CHX) treatment 60 min prior to rCD1 addition. As shown in Figure 7A and C, PI(4,5)P2 depletion resulted in loss of clusters from the PM that was fully reverted by restoring PI(4,5)P2 levels in the presence of CHX (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: Gag molecules synthesized before assembly site dissociation are sufficient for formation of new assembly sites following PI(4,5)P2 reconstitution and new protein synthesis is not required.
source: These data indicate that Gag molecules synthesized before assembly site dissociation are sufficient for formation of new assembly sites following PI(4,5)P2 reconstitution and new protein synthesis is not required.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the CHX experiments in Figure 7.

claim: Co-expression of Gag-EGFP(G2A) and wild-type Gag led to formation of fluorescent assembly sites at the PM.
source: Accordingly, co-expression of Gag-EGFP(G2A) and wild-type Gag (in 2:1 molar ratio) led to formation of fluorescent assembly sites at the PM (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A) of cells expressing the Anchor and Enzyme, while Gag-EGFP(G2A) alone failed to assemble.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Addition of rCD1 resulted in a loss of Gag-EGFP(G2A) clusters from the PM.
source: As expected, addition of rCD1 resulted in a loss of Gag-EGFP(G2A) clusters from the PM (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and C.

claim: Only few Gag-EGFP(G2A) clusters reformed at the PM and Gag-EGFP(G2A) was not efficiently re-recruited to the PM upon PI(4,5)P2 rescue.
source: However, only few Gag-EGFP(G2A) clusters reformed at the PM and the quantitative analysis revealed, that Gag-EGFP(G2A) was not efficiently re-recruited to the PM upon PI(4,5)P2 rescue (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B and D), while wild-type Gag readily formed new assembly sites under these conditions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B and D.

claim: The G2A result is consistent with complete dissociation of Gag clusters following PI(4,5)P2 depletion.
source: This result is consistent with complete dissociation of Gag clusters following PI(4,5)P2 depletion.
evidence: This is an inference from the G2A rescue experiments.

claim: Neither the size nor the fluorescence intensity of residual G2A clusters increased following PI(4,5)P2 restoration.
source: Quantitative analysis revealed that neither the size nor the fluorescence intensity of residual clusters increased following PI(4,5)P2 restoration (Figure 6—figure supplement 3E–H), arguing against recruitment of Gag(G2A) molecules to residual assembly sites.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3E-H.

claim: The mean assembly rate constant of k = 5.8 ± 0.6*10−3 s−1 for reinduced assembly was slightly, but significantly, increased compared to native assembly (native: k = 4.5 ± 0.5*10−3 s−1, p<0.0001).
source: The mean assembly rate constant of k = 5.8 ± 0.6*10−3 s−1 for reinduced assembly, which was derived from averaging all individual k values, was slightly, but significantly, increased compared to native assembly (native: k = 4.5 ± 0.5*10−3 s−1, p<0.0001) (Figure 6—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is quantitative data from Figure 6—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The assembly constant for reinduced assembly translates into a half-time of ~120 s (native: t1/2 ~150 s).
source: The assembly constant for reinduced assembly translates into a half-time of ~120 s (native: t1/2 ~150 s).
evidence: This is calculated from the assembly rate constants.

claim: The average assembly constant for native assembly at the lateral PM was k = 5.9 ± 0.4*10−3 s−1, which was very similar to that observed for reinduced assembly (no significant change, p=0.1569).
source: The average assembly constant derived from single exponential fits for all native assembly traces under these conditions of k = 5.9 ± 0.4*10−3 s−1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 4C) was very similar to that observed for reinduced assembly (no significant change, p=0.1569) and was again significantly faster than observed for assembly at the ventral membrane (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is quantitative data from Figure 6—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Native assembly at the lateral PM was significantly faster than observed for assembly at the ventral membrane (p<0.0001).
source: The average assembly constant derived from single exponential fits for all native assembly traces under these conditions of k = 5.9 ± 0.4*10−3 s−1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 4C) was very similar to that observed for reinduced assembly (no significant change, p=0.1569) and was again significantly faster than observed for assembly at the ventral membrane (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is quantitative data from Figure 6—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The observed difference in assembly rates between ventral and lateral PM may reflect effects of the adjacent glass substrate on the kinetics of HIV-1 Gag assembly.
source: The observed difference may reflect effects of the adjacent glass substrate on the kinetics of HIV-1 Gag assembly at the ventral membrane, but clearly shows that reinduced and native assembly site formation occur with very similar kinetics.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference.

claim: Reinduced and native assembly site formation occur with very similar kinetics.
source: The observed difference may reflect effects of the adjacent glass substrate on the kinetics of HIV-1 Gag assembly at the ventral membrane, but clearly shows that reinduced and native assembly site formation occur with very similar kinetics.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the assembly kinetics data.

claim: Late native HIV-1 assemblies at the lateral PM appeared very similar to those detected at the ventral PM.
source: As shown in Figure 8A, late native HIV-1 assemblies at the lateral PM appeared very similar to those detected at the ventral PM (compare Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown by comparison of Figures 8A and 4.

claim: Reinduced assembly sites displayed the distinct phenotype of condensed Gag clusters with a diameter of roughly 120 nm surrounded by larger Env clusters.
source: Reinduced assembly sites also displayed this distinct phenotype (Figure 8B) and were undistinguishable from native assembly sites at the lateral PM with respect to diameter and morphology in micrographs and line plot diagrams of Gag and Env (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B-D.

claim: Reinduced assembly sites were undistinguishable from native assembly sites at the lateral PM with respect to diameter and morphology.
source: Reinduced assembly sites also displayed this distinct phenotype (Figure 8B) and were undistinguishable from native assembly sites at the lateral PM with respect to diameter and morphology in micrographs and line plot diagrams of Gag and Env (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B-D.

claim: The rCDS has several advantages compared to alternative strategies for PI(4,5)P2 manipulation.
source: This rCDS has several advantages compared to alternative strategies. First, PI(4,5)P2 depletion is strictly dependent on rCD1 addition and can be rapidly achieved within minutes. This allows maintaining normal cell metabolism prior to compound addition despite the presence of all rCDS components in the cell, and should thus prevent induction of escape pathways. Second, the system is completely and rapidly reversible, allowing restoration of PM PI(4,5)P2 levels within minutes of FK506 addition.
evidence: This describes the advantages of the rCDS system.

claim: Long-term depletion of PM PI(4,5)P2 is compatible with cell viability and viral protein expression.
source: Here, we show that long-term depletion of PM PI(4,5)P2 is compatible with cell viability and viral protein expression, while completely preventing Gag membrane targeting and assembly site formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental results showing cells remain viable during extended PI(4,5)P2 depletion.

claim: Large clusters removed from the membrane appeared to dissociate into monomers or small oligomers in the cytosol.
source: Furthermore, PI(4,5)P2 depletion also caused loss of pre-assembled Gag lattices from the PM and large clusters removed from the membrane appeared to dissociate into monomers or small oligomers in the cytosol.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Gag becomes cytosolic and can reassemble.

claim: Rate constants for native and induced assembly, and even for reinduced assembly following depletion and subsequent restoration of PI(4,5)P2, are virtually identical.
source: Our results show that rate constants for native and induced assembly, and even for reinduced assembly following depletion and subsequent restoration of PI(4,5)P2, are virtually identical.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis in Figures 3 and 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is important to retain Gag once it reaches the PM, but does not affect its PM trafficking.
source: This observation is consistent with the assumption that PI(4,5)P2 is important to retain Gag once it reaches the PM, but does not affect its PM trafficking, which may be rate-limiting under these conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that assembly rates are similar but accumulation is faster under induced conditions.

claim: Gag assembly site formation was not faster, but more synchronous under induced or reinduced assembly conditions compared to native assembly.
source: Interestingly, Gag assembly site formation was not faster, but more synchronous under induced or reinduced assembly conditions compared to native assembly.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2-3.

claim: The more synchronous assembly likely reflects the presence of a large pool of assembly competent Gag in PI(4,5)P2 depleted cells.
source: This finding most likely reflects the presence of a large pool of assembly competent Gag in PI(4,5)P2 depleted cells, which can only be retained at the PM upon PI(4,5)P2 restoration.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the synchronous assembly observation.

claim: Gag molecules may transiently associate with all cellular membranes including the PM in the absence of PI(4,5)P2, but are stably retained only in the presence of this phosphoinositide.
source: Gag molecules may transiently associate with all cellular membranes including the PM in the absence of PI(4,5)P2, but are stably retained only in the presence of this phosphoinositide.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations.

claim: Assembly site formation is synchronized by the rCDS, which provides a promising tool to study the role of host components during HIV-1 assembly and the induction of virus maturation.
source: Assembly site formation therefore is synchronized by the rCDS, which provides a promising tool to study the role of host components during HIV-1 assembly and the induction of virus maturation.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the rCDS system.

claim: Virions released under induced conditions are infectious.
source: The observation that virions released under those conditions are infectious and the opportunity to use stable HeLarCDS cells for bulk assays broadens the range of applications for this system.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: The finding that PI(4,5)P2 is required to retain partially or completely assembled Gag lattices at the PM was unexpected.
source: The finding that PI(4,5)P2 is also required to retain partially or completely assembled Gag lattices at the PM was unexpected, since a triggered myristoyl switch in conjunction with ionic interactions between the HBR and negatively charged lipids of the inner leaflet would be expected to retain Gag at the PM, especially considering the high avidity of the multimeric Gag lattice (ca. 2,500 Gag molecules per assembly site).
evidence: This contrasts with expectations based on the myristoyl switch model.

claim: Large PM Gag clusters resembling fully assembled HIV-1 budding structures were rapidly and completely lost from the PM upon PI(4,5)P2 depletion.
source: Large PM Gag clusters resembling fully assembled HIV-1 budding structures were rapidly and completely lost from the PM upon PI(4,5)P2 depletion, however.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 is clearly required throughout assembly and budding of HIV-1 particles and not only for Gag membrane targeting.
source: Thus, PI(4,5)P2 is clearly required throughout assembly and budding of HIV-1 particles and not only for Gag membrane targeting.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that pre-assembled sites dissociate upon PI(4,5)P2 depletion.

claim: In vitro, MA binding to liposomes is significantly weaker for PI(4)P compared to PI(4,5)P2.
source: In vitro, MA binding to liposomes is significantly weaker for PI(4)P compared to PI(4,5)P2 (Mercredi et al., 2016), suggesting that Gag dissociation from the PM may be directly caused by dephosphorylation of PI(4,5)P2 and consequent loss of Gag interaction.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mercredi et al., 2016.

claim: Gag dissociation from the PM may be directly caused by dephosphorylation of PI(4,5)P2 and consequent loss of Gag interaction.
source: In vitro, MA binding to liposomes is significantly weaker for PI(4)P compared to PI(4,5)P2 (Mercredi et al., 2016), suggesting that Gag dissociation from the PM may be directly caused by dephosphorylation of PI(4,5)P2 and consequent loss of Gag interaction.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on in vitro data.

claim: It is not entirely clear whether Gag-associated phosphoinositides are good substrates for the phosphatase since the enzyme would have to enter the tight protein lattice of the assembling virion.
source: It is not entirely clear, however, whether Gag-associated phosphoinositides are good substrates for the phosphatase since the enzyme would have to enter the tight protein lattice of the assembling virion.
evidence: This raises a question about the mechanism of PI(4,5)P2 depletion at assembly sites.

claim: Effects of general depletion of PM PI(4,5)P2 with lipid exchange of Gag molecules must also be considered.
source: Accordingly, effects of general depletion of PM PI(4,5)P2 with lipid exchange of Gag molecules must also be considered.
evidence: This is an alternative explanation for the observed effects.

claim: The results are not easily reconciled with the suggested lipid flip model where the 2´acyl chain of PI(4,5)P2 would be pulled from the membrane and exchanged for the myristic acid.
source: Our results are not easily reconciled with the suggested lipid flip, where the 2´acyl chain of PI(4,5)P2 would be pulled from the membrane and exchanged for the myristic acid once the myristate switch is triggered.
evidence: This is a conclusion that the data are inconsistent with the lipid flip model.

claim: Extrusion of the 20-carbon 2´-acyl chain of PI(4,5)P2 would require ~24 kcal/mol.
source: As discussed by Summers and colleagues (Mercredi et al., 2016), extrusion of the 20-carbon 2´-acyl chain of PI(4,5)P2 would require ~24 kcal/mol (Tanford, 1979; Israelachvili et al., 1977), while inserting 10 carbons of myristate into the lipid bilayer would gain only 8 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is a thermodynamic calculation cited from previous work.

claim: Inserting 10 carbons of myristate into the lipid bilayer would gain only 8 kcal/mol.
source: As discussed by Summers and colleagues (Mercredi et al., 2016), extrusion of the 20-carbon 2´-acyl chain of PI(4,5)P2 would require ~24 kcal/mol (Tanford, 1979; Israelachvili et al., 1977), while inserting 10 carbons of myristate into the lipid bilayer would gain only 8 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is a thermodynamic calculation cited from previous work.

claim: The binding energy of the myristate anchor is not sufficient to retain individual Gag molecules at the PM.
source: While the binding energy of the myristate anchor is not sufficient to retain individual Gag molecules at the PM, the avidity effects of up to 2500 Gag molecules with all or the majority of their N-terminal myristate groups inserted into the inner leaflet should make membrane association of the Gag lattice almost irreversible, independent of PI(4,5)P2.
evidence: This is a thermodynamic argument about Gag membrane association.

claim: The avidity effects of up to 2500 Gag molecules with all or the majority of their N-terminal myristate groups inserted into the inner leaflet should make membrane association of the Gag lattice almost irreversible, independent of PI(4,5)P2.
source: While the binding energy of the myristate anchor is not sufficient to retain individual Gag molecules at the PM, the avidity effects of up to 2500 Gag molecules with all or the majority of their N-terminal myristate groups inserted into the inner leaflet should make membrane association of the Gag lattice almost irreversible, independent of PI(4,5)P2.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that is contradicted by the experimental results.

claim: The binding energy of myristate interaction with MA is the same as for extrusion of myristate from the PM (8 kcal/mol).
source: Given that the binding energy of myristate interaction with MA is the same as for extrusion of myristate from the PM (8 kcal/mol) (Charlier et al., 2014), we suggest a dynamic equilibrium between fully membrane-inserted and MA-bound PI(4,5)P2 molecules at the assembly site.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Charlier et al., 2014.

claim: A dynamic equilibrium exists between fully membrane-inserted and MA-bound PI(4,5)P2 molecules at the assembly site.
source: Given that the binding energy of myristate interaction with MA is the same as for extrusion of myristate from the PM (8 kcal/mol) (Charlier et al., 2014), we suggest a dynamic equilibrium between fully membrane-inserted and MA-bound PI(4,5)P2 molecules at the assembly site.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on thermodynamic considerations and experimental observations.

claim: Myristate may readily flip between the inner leaflet of the PM and the lipid binding pocket of MA.
source: Accordingly, myristate may readily flip between the inner leaflet of the PM and the lipid binding pocket of MA.
evidence: This is part of the proposed dynamic equilibrium model.

claim: Once Gag reaches the PM, PI(4,5)P2 association triggers the myristate switch, and this effect is enhanced by the presence of acidic phospholipids.
source: Once Gag reaches the PM, PI(4,5)P2 association triggers the myristate switch, and this effect is enhanced by the presence of acidic phospholipids.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model for Gag membrane association.

claim: The combination of specific PI(4,5)P2 binding and myristate insertion into the PM anchors the Gag molecule and makes it available for virus assembly.
source: The combination of specific PI(4,5)P2 binding and myristate insertion into the PM then anchors the Gag molecule and makes it available for virus assembly.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: A dynamic exchange of lipid interactions may occur, where depletion of PM PI(4,5)P2 causes loss of Gag molecules once their myristate moieties flip out from the membrane.
source: Subsequently, a dynamic exchange of lipid interactions may occur, where depletion of PM PI(4,5)P2 causes loss of Gag molecules once their myristate moieties flip out from the membrane.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism to explain the observed PI(4,5)P2 dependence of assembled Gag.

claim: Comparison of the membrane localization of Gag assembly sites prior to PI(4,5)P2 depletion with assembly sites after PI(4,5)P2 restoration indicated that they occur in different positions.
source: Finally, our results also shed some light on the question whether Gag assembly is directed to pre-existing assembly-prone membrane microdomains or whether Gag creates its own microdomain. Comparison of the membrane localization of Gag assembly sites prior to PI(4,5)P2 depletion with assembly sites in the same region of the cell after PI(4,5)P2 restoration indicated that they occur in different positions.
evidence: This is an observation from the microscopy experiments.

claim: There are no stable assembly-prone membrane microdomains.
source: The conclusion that there are no stable assembly-prone membrane microdomains is consistent with earlier observations showing that Gag initially binds to non-raft regions of the PM and subsequently either laterally associates with raft like domains or induces their formation (Ono and Freed, 2001; Mercredi et al., 2016).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that assembly sites form at different locations after PI(4,5)P2 restoration.

claim: Gag initially binds to non-raft regions of the PM and subsequently either laterally associates with raft like domains or induces their formation.
source: The conclusion that there are no stable assembly-prone membrane microdomains is consistent with earlier observations showing that Gag initially binds to non-raft regions of the PM and subsequently either laterally associates with raft like domains or induces their formation (Ono and Freed, 2001; Mercredi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The study shows that PI(4,5)P2 at the PM is crucial throughout the entire HIV-1 assembly process.
source: Collectively, our study shows that PI(4,5)P2 at the PM is crucial throughout the entire HIV-1 assembly process and suggests a dynamic equilibrium of Gag-lipid interactions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The study establishes an experimental system that permits synchronized induction of HIV-1 assembly by targeted modulation of Gag PM targeting.
source: Furthermore, it establishes an experimental system that permits synchronized induction of HIV-1 assembly by targeted modulation of Gag PM targeting.
evidence: This is a key outcome of the study.
